text: The glassworks opened in the spring of that year. The owners brought money from the city. The workers came in from the nearby farms. The furnace burned day and night all year. The town grew up around the works.
strengths: every fact is clear on its own
weaknesses: five sentences of seven to nine words
every sentence has the same subject, verb, object shape
nothing is connected, so nothing builds
spokenRhythm: A metronome, five matching beats with the same fall at the end of each.
narrativeFunction: Tries to set up a factory town but sounds like a list read aloud.
whyItFails: When every sentence is the same length and shape, the ear stops listening for meaning and starts hearing the pattern. The facts are fine, but none of them is linked to another, so the money, the workers and the furnace never become cause and effect. A voice reading this sounds bored, and so does the audience.
rewrite: The glassworks opened in the spring of that year, on money the owners brought from the city. Its workers came in from the nearby farms. The furnace burned day and night all year, and the town grew up around the works.

text: One ship. One cargo. One chance. The vessel carried nutmeg worth more than its weight in silver. Two years at sea. Storms. Pirates. Disease. Only a third of the crew came home.
strengths: the closing fact about the crew is strong on its own
weaknesses: seven fragments in a short passage
worth more than its weight in silver bends a stock phrase
the dangers are listed, never explained
spokenRhythm: A string of hard stops, like a trailer voice counting down, with one full sentence lost in the middle.
narrativeFunction: Tries to make a spice voyage sound dangerous through punctuation.
whyItFails: Fragments in a run are the most recognisable rhythm of machine-written history. Each full stop asks for drama, so after the third one the listener hears the technique instead of the voyage. Storms, pirates and disease become a word cloud rather than events that happened to people.
rewrite: The ship carried nutmeg that was worth more than silver, weight for weight. In two years at sea the crew faced storms, pirates and disease, and only a third of them came home.

text: The ice trade changed everything — ice that once melted in days now lasted for months — and the merchants who saw it first — the ones who built the ice houses — made their fortunes almost overnight.
strengths: contains a real point about storage and timing
weaknesses: two pairs of dashes in one sentence
the main clause is broken twice before it finishes
changed everything announces instead of explaining
almost overnight is a stock phrase that claims speed without a date
spokenRhythm: A breathless sentence that stops and restarts four times, so the voice never finds a resting place.
narrativeFunction: Tries to explain why the ice trade paid but hides the explanation inside asides.
whyItFails: Em-dashes are a page device. Aloud, the listener has to hold the opening clause across two interruptions, and a voice reading it either rushes the asides or loses the thread. The facts that matter, how long the ice lasted and who profited, are buried in the parentheses while the headline is an empty claim.
rewrite: Ice that had once melted in days now lasted for months. The merchants who saw that first, and built the ice houses, made their fortunes quickly.

text: What did a quarryman earn for a day on the slate face? Two shillings. Was it enough? Not even close. The result? A strike that shut every quarry in the valley for six months.
strengths: the wage and the length of the strike are both concrete
weaknesses: three questions the narrator answers at once
not even close is a judgement with no evidence
spokenRhythm: Question, snap answer, question, snap answer, a call-and-response that sounds like a quiz show.
narrativeFunction: Tries to explain a wage dispute by staging it as a series of questions.
whyItFails: A narrator who asks and answers his own questions is performing curiosity rather than sharing it. The question-and-fragment pattern is a machine cadence, and three of them in a row turn a serious dispute into a game. Not even close is a verdict with no evidence behind it, and the wage never gets the context that would let a listener judge it. The house version can only drop the performance, since the bad text supplies no comparison.
rewrite: A quarryman earned two shillings for a day on the slate face, and it was nowhere near enough. The strike that followed shut every quarry in the valley for six months.

text: The telegraph office opened in the spring. And then the first messages arrived from the capital. And then the express riders lost their work. And then the courier company sold its horses. But this was only the beginning.
strengths: the chain of consequences is a good one
weaknesses: three sentences opening with And then
the same length and shape again and again
ends on a tease that promises nothing specific
spokenRhythm: A sing-song chain where every sentence starts on the same two words and falls the same way.
narrativeFunction: Tries to show the knock-on effects of the telegraph but sounds like a child retelling a story.
whyItFails: Repeated openings make the rhythm predictable, and And then adds fake momentum to events that already follow from one another. The closing line is a micro hook that sells the next section instead of ending this one. The consequences are interesting, and the shape of the sentences hides them.
rewrite: The telegraph office opened in the spring. After the first messages arrived from the capital, the express riders lost their work, and the courier company sold its horses.
